<!-- Numbers from analysis/4_memory.qmd, "Durability" (Beauty2Recognition, Beauty2Reality; data/results_memory_durability.csv): label contrasts within recognized / unrecognized artworks (% of the slider; P(beautiful side) in percentage points), the recognition contrast, the slope of follow-up beauty on the Phase-2 syntheticness belief per label (per +10% of the belief slider, Phase-1 beauty at the participant's mean) and the indirect effect of the label through that belief. The "Total" / "Direct" rows of that model condition on the label-depressed Phase-1 beauty and are not label effects (see the notebook). -->

Two further models looked for what this null might hide. First, a residual label effect appeared only among the artworks that participants still recognized (43.1% of those seen in Phase 1), and only on the categorical component of the judgment: recognized artworks previously labelled as AI-Generated were somewhat less likely to be placed on the "beautiful" side of the scale than recognized Originals (-4.6% [-9.1, -0.3]), whereas unrecognized ones were not. Second, the syntheticness belief formed in Phase 2 carried into the follow-up: given the Phase 1 beauty of an artwork, the more human-made a participant had judged it to be, the more beautiful they found it six weeks later, so that the AI label retained a small indirect effect on follow-up beauty through the belief it had induced (-0.3% [-0.4, -0.1]). The trace that the label left in the aesthetic judgment itself was thus small and confined to the artworks that participants still recognized; it was clearer in the belief about the artwork, which in turn still coloured its later appreciation.

### Memory for Labels and Beliefs

<!-- Numbers from analysis/4_memory.qmd (data/results_memory_contrasts.csv, results_memory_means.csv): categorical models of the recalled label (MemoryCondition), of the recalled own belief (MemoryBelief), and of the recalled label by own belief with the label shown held constant (MemoryConditionBelief); recognition and recalled label by Phase-1 beauty and valence (MemoryAppraisal, data/results_memory_appraisal.csv: population-level predictions at -2 / -1 / +1 / +2 SD minus at the participant's mean, recognition = 1 - P(Not recognized), labels given recognition; "joint" rows move the other rating along its within-person regression, "unique" rows hold it at 0; item-level correlations from 4_memory.qmd); differences of probabilities (over all items, "Not recognized" included) in percentage points. Percentages "of the recognized artworks" are descriptive (data_memory_task.csv). -->

Participants recognized 43.1% of the artworks seen in Phase 1, against a false-alarm rate of 11.1% for new artworks. Recognition did not depend on the label under which an artwork had been presented, nor on the participant's own Phase 2 belief about it, but on how the artwork had been appraised in Phase 1. In line with our previous work linking extreme aesthetic judgments to a mnemonic advantage [@lee2023; @salgues2024], we had hypothesized that artworks receiving extreme ratings, whether positive or negative, would be better remembered. This held for the positive extreme only: artworks rated as more beautiful than the participant's average (and, as the two ratings usually went together, as more positive) were more likely to be recognized, increasingly so toward the top of the range (+12.0% [6.9, 17.3] at two SD above the participant's mean; @fig-4, bottom), whereas artworks rated as less beautiful than average were not (+0.0% [-4.1, 4.2] at two SD below). Of the two ratings, only beauty retained a credible effect when each was varied with the other held constant. The artworks with the highest recognition rates were nonetheless the ugliest and most negative ones, but this was a property of the artworks (those of higher normative arousal, and those found uglier on average, were better recognized by everyone), which the model separates from each participant's own appraisal: within a given artwork, it was finding it more beautiful than usual, not finding it extreme, that made it more memorable.

<!-- Numbers from analysis/6_selfrelevance.qmd, section (C), MemorySR (data/results_selfrelevance_memory.csv): P("seen before") at -2 / +2 SD of the rating minus at the participant's mean, for old items (hits, averaged over the three labels) and new items (false alarms), percentage points, and the same as log odds ratios. "unique" rows (the other rating at the participant's mean). -->

Self-relevance, rated at follow-up, was also related to recognition, but not in the way a self-reference effect would predict. More self-relevant artworks were more often reported as "seen before", but as much when they were new as when they had actually been seen (@fig-4, bottom right): the effect was larger in percentage points for old artworks only because hits were far more frequent than false alarms, and on the odds scale it did not differ between old and new artworks (difference in log-odds ratio at two SD above the mean: -0.11 [-0.38, 0.16]). The same held for follow-up beauty. Self-relevance and beauty at follow-up thus indexed a bias to judge a resonant or appealing artwork as familiar rather than better memory for it, which is why the Phase 1 appraisal (rated before any memory judgment, and only for artworks actually seen) is the cleaner index of what was encoded.

Memory for the label itself was at chance: artworks were no more often attributed the label they had actually carried than any other label (all differences ≤ 1.3 percentage points, all CIs including 0). Instead, label attributions followed a stable response bias: whatever their actual label, recognized artworks were most often remembered as being associated with the "Original" label (51% of recognized artworks), followed by "AI-Generated" (33%) and "Forgery" (15%). New artworks that were falsely recognized received the same distribution of labels (53%, 32% and 15%), suggesting that label attributions were reconstructed rather than retrieved. The preference for the Original label may be partly driven by the reminder, at the start of the follow-up session, that all artworks were genuine human originals.

In contrast, participants' recollection of their own Phase 2 belief was above chance, mainly along the syntheticness dimension (@fig-4, top). Artworks that a participant had judged to be AI originals were more often recalled as such than artworks judged to be Human Originals (+6.5% [4.7, 8.5]), and less often recalled as Human Originals (-8.0% [-9.9, -6.2]), whereas artworks judged to be Forgeries were not more often recalled as Forgeries than those judged to be Originals, nor were AI copies more often recalled as AI copies. As the model included participant- and item-level variability in each answer, this correspondence is not a matter of general response tendencies, or of some artworks looking more artificial than others to everyone.

<!-- Numbers from analysis/4_memory.qmd, "Memory or Re-inference? Controlling for the Appraisal" (MemoryBeliefAppraisal, MemoryConditionAppraisal): Belief contrasts with the three ratings in the model (percentage points over all items), and the rating effects at -2 / +2 SD of the rating minus at the participant's mean, among recognized artworks, other ratings at the mean. -->

This correspondence may, however, reflect a stable, personal impression of an artwork re-expressed at follow-up as much as an episodic memory of the past judgment: beauty and self-relevance were rated again immediately before the memory questions, and beauty was closely associated with the belief in Phase 2. It nonetheless survived when the current impression was taken into account: with the Phase 1 beauty, follow-up beauty and self-relevance of the artwork in the model, the belief effects were unchanged (artworks judged to be AI originals recalled as such: +7.1% [5.2, 9.0]), although the current impression shaped the answers on its own, artworks currently found more beautiful being more often recalled as Human Originals (+10.7% [6.8, 15.3] of recognized artworks at two SD above the participant's mean), as were, to a lesser extent, more self-relevant ones. The recalled belief was thus both a memory of the Phase 2 judgment and a re-inference from the present appraisal, the two contributing independently.

<!-- Recalled label by Phase 1 appraisal: MemoryAppraisal (analysis/4_memory.qmd, data/results_memory_appraisal.csv, "joint" rows, P(label | recognised) at -2 / +2 SD minus at the mean, in percentage points); with the belief, follow-up beauty and self-relevance held constant: MemoryConditionAppraisal ("unique" rating effects among recognized artworks); self-relevance on the recalled label among recognized old artworks: MemorySR (analysis/6_selfrelevance.qmd, section C, data/results_selfrelevance_memory.csv). The two appraisal estimates come from differently specified models (beauty and valence moved jointly vs. beauty alone, with the follow-up ratings in the model), so their difference is not a formal decomposition. -->

The recalled label, in turn, appeared to be reconstructed from this belief and from the Phase 1 appraisal (@fig-4, top and bottom). With the label actually shown held constant, artworks that a participant had judged to be AI originals were more often attributed the "AI-Generated" label than those judged to be Human Originals (+7.0% [5.0, 8.9]; among recognized artworks: 43.6% vs. 27.3%), again along the syntheticness dimension only (artworks judged to be Forgeries were not more often attributed the "Forgery" label). The "beautiful = human" inference described above also entered this reconstruction: artworks rated as less beautiful than the participant's average in Phase 1 were more often remembered as "AI-Generated" (+7.4% [1.8, 12.7] of recognized artworks at two SD below the mean) and those rated as more beautiful more often as "Original", whereas the "Forgery" attribution did not follow beauty. This effect was smaller, but still present, with the belief, follow-up beauty and self-relevance held constant, and it was the Phase 1 appraisal rather than the current one that mattered, follow-up beauty having no effect. Self-relevance acted in the same direction, more self-relevant recognized artworks being more often attributed the "Original" label and less often the "AI-Generated" label. In other words, participants remembered what they had come to believe about an artwork, and what they had felt about it in Phase 1, but not what they had been told about it.


## Interindividual Differences

<!-- Numbers from analysis/7_correlates.qmd: reliability (D-vour) tables of the participant-level and memory indices, "Correlations between participant-level indices", "Hierarchical EGA: community membership and item stability", "Number of communities across bootstraps"; network loadings and correlations between community scores from the cached EGA fit (ega$parameters$lower_loadings, net.loads(ega$higher_order), net.scores()); max |r| of the recall tendencies with all 64 Phase 1 / Phase 2 indices computed from models/individual/ (2026-09-26 check). Community scores are oriented so that a higher score = more of what the label says (7_correlates.qmd, "Orientation", 2026-09-26): anti-fake bias and ugliness extremity are reversed relative to the raw network loadings (a higher anti-fake bias score = a larger penalty; a higher ugliness extremity score = more extreme ugliness judgments), and the aesthetic appraisal higher-order score is oriented so that ugliness extremity, its dominant community, loads positively. The higher-order scores are not shown in the lower panel of the figure (r = .97-.99 with their dominant communities). -->

Participants differed reliably in their baseline responses, but much less in their sensitivity to the labels. All baseline indices were reliable (D-vour from .58 to .97), whereas individual differences in the label effects were mostly dominated by estimation uncertainty: the effect of the AI-Generated label was moderately reliable on the Phase 1 ratings (.34 to .71), the effect of the Forgery label only on worth (.55), and none of the label effects on the Phase 2 beliefs was (all ≤ .13). With 16 artworks per label and participant, the latter result does not show that participants did not differ in how the labels shifted their beliefs, but that such differences, if any, were too small to be measured with this design. The "beautiful = human" slope was moderately reliable (.44).

The 28 baseline and label-effect indices with a reliability above 1/3 formed nine lower-order communities, grouped into three higher-order communities (@fig-5, top). The first, *aesthetic appraisal*, gathered the Phase 1 indices into four communities: *aesthetic sensitivity*, the baseline level of the four ratings (finding the Originals beautiful, pleasant, meaningful and valuable); *anti-fake bias*, the effects of the AI-Generated label on the four ratings and of the Forgery label on worth; *rating consistency*, the precision of the four ratings; and *ugliness extremity*, how far into the "ugly" side of the beauty scale participants went when they chose that side. The anti-fake bias thus formed a dimension of its own, largely independent of how much participants appreciated the artworks in general (*r* = .17). The Phase 2 indices formed the two other higher-order communities: *realness beliefs*, comprising the baseline tendency to judge the artworks as human-made and original (*realness tendency*) and the extremity of these judgments on the human / original side (*realness conviction*) and on the AI / copy side (*fakeness conviction*), and *belief consistency*, comprising the precision of the judgments on either side. Each Phase 2 community paired a syntheticness index with its authenticity counterpart: the extremity and precision of the two beliefs were strongly correlated, whereas the tendencies to judge the artworks as human-made and as original were only weakly related, so that participants differed in a shared way of using the two belief scales rather than in a general belief that the artworks were fake. As each higher-order score was dominated by one or two of its lower-order communities (*r* = .97 to .99), we report the correlates of the lower-order communities only. This structure was moderately stable: across 500 bootstrap samples, three higher-order communities were found in 56% of the samples, and nine lower-order communities was the most frequent solution (31%).

Two further sets of indices were kept out of this structure. The "beautiful = human" slope was nearly unrelated to all other indices and to all participant characteristics (all |*r*| ≤ .18). At follow-up, the tendencies to attribute each label to recognized artworks were reliable individual characteristics (D-vour .69 to .80), unlike the accuracy of these attributions (.09), but they were unrelated to all Phase 1 and Phase 2 indices (all |*r*| ≤ .17): how inclined a participant was to attribute each label was unrelated to how they had, overall, appraised the artworks and judged their origin (at the level of the artworks, by contrast, the attributions followed the appraisal and the belief; see Memory for Labels and Beliefs).

#| label: fig-5

#| out-width: "100%"

## Dispositional Correlates

<!-- Numbers from analysis/7_correlates.qmd, "Manuscript figure: correlations between participant characteristics and community scores and label recall tendencies" (Markdown table; df_correlates_ms: 28 characteristics x 7 lower-order community scores + 3 recall tendencies, FDR over its 280 cells; n = 324 minus questionnaire exclusions, 317 for Phase 2 scores, 220 for the recall tendencies). Scores oriented so that higher = more of the label (anti-fake bias: larger penalty). Within the 84 trait x recall correlations alone, no FDR-corrected p < .05 (smallest .12; 2026-09-26 check). VVIQ_Total higher = more vivid since the 2026-09-26 fix in 1_cleaning.qmd (it was reverse-scored before). The sentence on which part of the penalty carries the attitude association (2026-10-19): 7_correlates.qmd, "Generic and AI-specific penalties and attitudes toward AI" (participant-level Forgery, AI and AI - Forgery mu indices vs the three BAIT scales; in words only). -->

The community scores and the label recall tendencies were then correlated with the participants' characteristics (@fig-5, bottom). As preregistered, the anti-fake bias was related to attitudes toward AI, and to no other characteristic after correction: participants with more negative attitudes toward AI penalized the non-original labels more strongly (*r* = .36), whereas those who believed that AI-generated art can rival human art (*r* = -.37) and those with more positive attitudes toward AI (*r* = -.25) penalized them less. This association was carried by the part of the penalty specific to the AI label: the participant-level effect of the Forgery label was largely unrelated to attitudes toward AI, whereas the increment from the Forgery to the AI label was related to all three attitude scales. Contrary to the preregistered predictions, the bias was not larger in participants with higher interoceptive sensibility (all |*r*| ≤ .10), and its association with more vivid visual imagery was weak (*r* = .12) and did not survive the correction. The bias was also unrelated to manipulation distrust, art expertise, and knowledge and use of AI tools.

Interoceptive sensibility was instead related to the baseline level of the judgments: participants reporting more interoceptive awareness and visceroception found the Originals more beautiful, pleasant, meaningful and valuable, as did participants with more art expertise, more knowledge and use of AI, more positive attitudes toward AI and more vivid visual imagery. Interoceptive sensibility also went with more decisive reality beliefs: participants reporting more interoceptive awareness made more extreme syntheticness and authenticity judgments, both on the human / original side (realness conviction: *r* = .26) and on the AI / copy side (fakeness conviction: *r* = .21), as did those reporting more visceroception, using AI tools more often and holding more positive attitudes toward AI. This association was specific to the reality judgments, which participants had been asked to make on "gut feeling" (interoceptive sensibility was unrelated to the extremity of ugliness judgments), and may reflect a greater reliance on, or confidence in, felt impressions. Finally, participants with more art expertise and more knowledge and use of AI tools rated the artworks less consistently from one artwork to the next. The ugliness extremity and realness tendency scores had no correlate surviving the correction.

At follow-up, the tendency to attribute the "Original" label to recognized artworks was higher in older participants (*r* = .20) and lower in participants who used AI tools more often (*r* = -.22). These associations are small, and survived the correction only as part of the whole set of correlations, but they are consistent with the reconstructive nature of label memory (see Memory for Labels and Beliefs): in the absence of a memory of the label, participants' attributions may follow their prior expectations about how common AI-generated images are.

# Discussion

<!-- Drafted 2026-10-18 from the bullet points collected while writing the Results, and tightened the same day (the first draft is in git history). No new estimates: every claim refers to a result reported in the Results, and numbers are kept out of the Discussion. -->

Is art devalued when attributed to AI because it is not an authentic original, or because it was not made by a human at all? By presenting the same genuine paintings as Originals, Forgeries or AI-Generated, we separated these two components and followed the bias from the moment of judgment to what remained of it six weeks later. Forgeries were judged less beautiful, less pleasant, less meaningful and less valuable than Originals, and AI-Generated works about twice as much so, whatever the emotional content of the painting and without any change in how it was looked at. Asked afterwards about each artwork's origin, participants judged those labelled AI-Generated as more synthetic and, less clearly, those labelled Forgeries as less original. These beliefs also followed participants' own aesthetic appraisal: the more beautiful they had found an artwork, the more likely they were to judge it human-made and original, and the link with human origin held even for newly presented artworks. Six weeks later, participants no longer showed the bias and forgot the labels. What they remembered, and attributed to the label, was what they had believed and felt.

## Not All Fakes Are Equally Ugly

The intermediate position of Forgeries shows that the anti-AI bias is partly a generic penalty for non-original works and partly specific to algorithmic authorship. A human copy was devalued on every dimension, as contagion accounts predict for an object that lacks the trace of its author [@newman2012; @huang2011]. The AI-specific component is not, however, a stronger version of the non-originality penalty: the AI label lowered judged authenticity no more than the Forgery label, and only through the poorer aesthetic appraisal it induced, whereas it made the artworks look more synthetic directly. What the AI label adds is the absence of a human author, in line with accounts that tie the value of a work to the human effort [@kruger2004effort] and intentions [@jucker2014just; @bullot2013artful] it is taken to embody, both of which a forger retains and an algorithm lacks.

This added penalty was the heaviest for meaning. Meaningfulness was the rating the AI label lowered most, the only one for which the increment from the Forgery to the AI label exceeded the penalty the two labels shared, and the only one the AI label drove to outright denial (answering the lower extreme - "0", to the meaning scale), a response the Forgery label barely touched. This matches the observation that the anti-AI bias is largest for judgments that attribute meaning, intention or depth to a work [@deroij2025], and the idea that meaning presupposes an agent whose intentions the work expresses: a forgery reproduces the content, and with it some of the meaning, that an artist put into the original, whereas a work attributed to an algorithm can be denied meaning altogether. In the terms of @leder2004model, the label acts at the stages of cognitive mastering and evaluation, where a work is interpreted in light of its presumed author, not at perceptual analysis. Consistent with this, the labels left visual exploration unchanged, as they left physiological responses unchanged in @chiarella2022, and as expected if the bias grows under reflective processing [@wang2026]. The gaze differences reported by @zhou2023 arose between paintings that participants had themselves classified as human- or AI-made, and may reflect the visual properties that drove the classification, which a randomly assigned label does not carry. Webcam eye tracking is coarse, and although its features did track the ratings (see Methods), this absence of effect should be interpreted with caution.

Is there such a thing as an anti-AI bias? Our results indicate about half of what the AI label cost was also paid by a human forgery, a penalty for works that are not their author's own, documented long before AI [@newman2012]; the other half was specific to the absence of a human author and was encoded as the dimension of "syntheticness" rather than as a further lack of authenticity. The devaluation is thus better described as an "authorship premium", which likely draws from two sides of authorship, the making of a work and its maker. The making, the effort, skill and creative conception a work is believed to embody, mostly depends on there being a maker, not on who that maker is. The maker, in turn, is a source from whom a work inherits the regard in which they are held, as objects do from contact with admired or despised people [@newman2011celebrity] and paintings from the name attached to them [@mastandrea2019peripheral; @kaube2024negative], and the penalty specific to AI did grow with negative attitudes toward it. The converse manipulation, varying the making while holding the maker constant, suggests that the making counts only when credited to a mind: making an AI take longer to generate an image led people to credit it with more effort, but not to appreciate the image more, appreciation following instead their attitudes toward AI and the consciousness they attributed to it [@theirs2026effort]. Varying the maker while holding the making constant would complete the picture: if the same image were rated higher when attributed to a new, acclaimed model than to an older, less regarded one, it would confirm that part of what is called an anti-AI bias is a contagion from a disliked maker rather than a judgment about how the work was made.

## Affect Shapes the Judgment but Not the Bias

The affective profile of an artwork shaped the judgments but not the bias. Negative, high-intensity works were judged far less beautiful and pleasant yet more meaningful, and the label effects were nonetheless present, in the same direction and of similar size, in every emotion category: the labels added a penalty on top of a work's affective profile rather than acting through it. Nor was there any sign that the AI label acted as a cue of unreality that dampens the emotional response, as in fictional reappraisal [@sperduti2016; @makowski2019]. Such dampening would have made negative works less unpleasant under the AI label; instead, the labels lowered valence in every category, negative works included. Self-reported valence, which earlier studies found insensitive to authorship [@zhou2023; @demmer2023], was thus affected here, but as a downward shift comparable to that of beauty, not as a blunting of the response. This does not rule out a dampening, however. Within an artistic frame, even scenes of martyrdom, war or death are depictions held at a distance, whose negative emotions can be savoured rather than avoided [@menninghaus2017distancing], and the valence ratings, although the question asked how the artwork made participants feel, may have recorded how sad or dark a work was more than an unpleasant feeling that a cue of unreality would down-regulate. Whether an AI label dampens the response to genuinely aversive material, such as the distressing scenes used in research on fictional reappraisal, remains to be tested. The drop in valence under the fake labels may likewise reflect a judgment about the artwork more than a change in how it made participants feel, in line with the absence of physiological effects of an AI label [@chiarella2022] and with a bias that operates through explicit, deliberate judgment [@bara2025].

## Labels, Appraisal, and Beliefs About Origin

The two fake labels were not encoded as one undifferentiated sense of fakeness. The AI label made artworks look more synthetic than both Originals and Forgeries, mostly directly. The Forgery label had a smaller effect on authenticity, not significantly larger than that of the AI label, but the only one with a direct component. Each label thus shifted directly the belief dimension it semantically implied, and spilled over onto the other dimension only through the poorer appraisal it induced; both direct effects acted on which side of the scale participants chose, not on their confidence within that side. The dissociation is asymmetric: the AI label was a strong and specific cue, the Forgery label a weak one. A copy has no perceptible signature when the original is unknown, whereas people hold expectations about what AI images look like. Accordingly, the style and normative arousal of the artworks predicted syntheticness, whereas nothing predicted authenticity, and across participants the two beliefs shared a response style but not a content: those inclined to judge the artworks human-made were not particularly inclined to judge them original. Because participants had been told that only some labels had been randomized, these effects reflect the sensible use of a partially valid cue rather than the persistence of a belief against its correction.

Aesthetic appraisal, in turn, informed belief. As preregistered, the more beautiful participants found an artwork, the more likely they judged it human-made and original, and this association needed no label: at follow-up, the more beautiful an artwork judged as new, the less likely it was rated AI-generated, including for new artworks that had never been labelled. The same inference has been observed for faces, attractive faces being less often judged artificial [@makowski2025too], and it extends to provenance the halo by which the beautiful is assumed to be good [@dion1972beautiful]. It has two consequences. Under a label, it closes a loop: the label lowers the appraisal, and the lower appraisal confirms the artificial origin, with about a third of the effect of the AI label on syntheticness manifesting this way. Without a label, appeal itself becomes evidence of origin, so that appealing AI images may pass as human-made, as AI-generated faces do [@nightingale2022ai; @miller2023ai], and human works that fail to please may be dismissed as AI-generated. The direction of the association remains an interpretation: an impression that a work looks artificial can form during viewing and lower its beauty, and a spontaneous, label-free anti-AI bias at the level of the artwork would produce the same pattern. Controlling for follow-up beauty excluded stable preferences for particular artworks as a common cause, not stable impressions of their artificiality. On either reading, aesthetic appraisal and beliefs about provenance are entangled for images of unknown origin, and the inference rests on the viewer's own appraisal rather than on a work's normative appeal, which did not predict syntheticness.

Of the four ratings, only beauty and meaningfulness carried unique parts of the label effects on beliefs; valence and worth, although lowered as much, did not. The route from appraisal to belief thus runs through evaluative and semantic judgment rather than through affect or economic value. Meaningfulness was both the rating the AI label depressed most and one of the two carrying its effect on belief, which suggests a two-way link between attributing meaning and attributing a human author: the AI label leads viewers to deny a work meaning, and a work that feels meaningless is taken to be AI-generated.

## Self-Relevance: A Cue to Human Origin, Not a Shield Against the Label

Self-relevance did not moderate the bias. Artworks that participants found more self-relevant had been judged more beautiful and meaningful, but the gap between labels was the same for them as for less self-relevant ones, within and between participants and for the categorical components of the judgments alike. Synthetic images personalized around a viewer's own memories and identity can be as appealing as human art [@vessel2023]; personal resonance with a given work, however, did not protect it from the devaluation that follows from attributing it to an algorithm or a forger. Two features of the design temper this conclusion. The artworks were not selected for personal relevance, and many were rated as not self-relevant at all, so that the autobiographical resonance produced by personalization was rarely reached; and self-relevance was rated at follow-up, after the debrief, as a stable property of the relation between viewer and work rather than while the label was present.

Self-relevance nonetheless played a role of its own in beliefs about origin. Beyond both beauty ratings, more self-relevant artworks were judged more human-made under the AI label and more original under the two fake labels, were less likely to be rated AI-generated when judged new at follow-up, and were more often remembered as Originals than as AI-Generated. Viewers appear to infer that a work that speaks to their own experience was made by someone with experiences of their own, a "self-relevant = human" inference that complements the "beautiful = human" one. In memory, by contrast, self-relevance produced no self-reference effect: it raised "seen before" answers as much for new as for old artworks, a familiarity bias rather than better memory. Unlike in studies that assessed self-relevance at encoding [@lee2023; @salgues2024], it was rated here at retrieval, where it may itself feed on a feeling of familiarity. The appraisal made at encoding did predict recognition, but on the positive side only: artworks rated as more beautiful than the participant's average were better remembered, those rated as less beautiful were not, which only partly supports a mnemonic advantage of extreme aesthetic judgments.

## What Remains of the Label

About six weeks later, reminded that all artworks were human originals, participants no longer rated previously AI- or Forgery-labelled artworks as less beautiful, more artificial or less self-relevant. The effect on beauty fell to about a tenth of its Phase 1 size. The bias thus behaves mainly as an online inference from the information at hand, not as a lasting encoding of the work, and in this differs from the perseverance of beliefs after debriefing [@ross1975perseverance] and from the continued influence of corrected misinformation [@lewandowsky2012misinformation], at least as far as the aesthetic judgment itself is concerned. Because time, correction and attrition are confounded in this design, the fading cannot be credited to the correction.

In the follow-up ratings, what persisted was the belief the label had induced more than its evaluative penalty. A residual penalty appeared only for artworks that participants still recognized, and only on the categorical choice between ugly and beautiful, the component through which the labels had shifted beliefs in Phase 2. And the syntheticness belief formed in Phase 2 carried over: given its Phase 1 beauty, an artwork that a participant had judged more human-made was found more beautiful six weeks later, so that the AI label kept a small indirect hold on appreciation through the belief it had created.

What participants explicitly remembered showed the same dissociation between the label and the belief it induced, more starkly. They did not remember which label an artwork had carried: their attributions were at chance and followed a response bias toward the Original label, perhaps encouraged by the reminder that all artworks were genuine. They did remember what they had believed, along the syntheticness dimension at least, beyond what their current impression of the work could explain, and they reconstructed the label from this belief and from their Phase 1 appraisal: artworks they had judged AI-generated, or had found less beautiful, were more often remembered as labelled AI-Generated. In the terms of the source-monitoring framework [@johnson1993source], the content of the belief survived while its source was lost, and the source was then inferred from the content: participants attributed to the label what they had concluded themselves. For the disclosure of AI-generated content, this means that a label may be forgotten within weeks while the beliefs it shaped remain, and that the labels people remember having seen reflect their own conclusions as much as the information they were given. For research, it means that delayed checks of a labelling manipulation measure beliefs as much as memory for the labels.

## An Attitude, Not a Sensitivity

Participants differed reliably in their baseline judgments but much less in their sensitivity to the labels. The effect of the AI label was a moderately reliable individual characteristic, that of the Forgery label only on worth, and individual differences in the label effects on beliefs could not be resolved with sixteen artworks per label; studies of individual differences in the bias will need many more trials, especially for beliefs. Where it could be measured, the anti-fake bias formed a dimension of its own, largely independent of how much participants appreciated the artworks, and was related, as preregistered, to attitudes toward AI and to nothing else: participants with more negative attitudes toward AI, and those who denied that AI-generated art can rival human art, penalized the fake labels more, whereas art expertise, knowledge and use of AI tools, and distrust of the manipulation played no role. The bias follows what people think about AI, not what they know about art, as a belief-driven account predicts.

Contrary to our preregistered predictions, neither interoceptive sensibility nor the vividness of visual imagery was related to the bias. Interoceptive sensibility was related instead to the baseline: participants reporting more interoceptive awareness found the artworks more beautiful, pleasant, meaningful and valuable, in line with work linking aesthetic experience to interoception [@cabbai2023; @washizu2025], and made more decisive reality judgments on both sides of the scales. In the Choice-Confidence model, this decisiveness is the confidence component of the judgment, how far toward the end of the chosen side the response goes. Work on interoception and metacognition suggests that confidence not only draws on sensory evidence but on bodily states as well [see @allen2016unexpected; @banellis2026interoceptive; @banellis2025mental]. Interoception questionnaires may therefore partly measure a general confidence in, or reliance on, one's felt impressions, which would show wherever a judgment is explicitly left to gut feeling, as the reality judgments were. As in interoceptive tasks, this confidence came without accuracy: all artworks were human originals, yet participants reporting more interoceptive awareness were also more convinced when they judged an artwork AI-generated or a copy. Response styles can produce spurious correlations between questionnaires and confidence ratings [@sarna2026biased], but this one was specific to the reality judgments (interoceptive sensibility was unrelated to the extremity of ugliness judgments), and the questionnaire data of inattentive participants had been discarded. Interoception may thus shape how strongly people engage with art and how confidently they judge its origin.

## Distinct Dimensions of Aesthetic Experience

Subjective aesthetic dimensions are often highly correlated and collapsed into a single appreciation factor. The present data argue for keeping them apart. Beauty, valence, meaning and worth map onto distinct processes, from sensory evaluation to affect, semantic processing and reward, and each showed a distributional signature of its own: valence symmetric and unimodal; meaningfulness zero-inflated, as if works were first gated as having meaning or none; worth right-skewed and decaying, as in economic valuation; beauty bimodal, combining polarized judgment with the anchoring that analog sliders invite. Response formats contributed to these shapes, but the results support the distinction: the labels lowered meaningfulness most and drove it to outright denial, and only beauty and meaningfulness carried the label effects on beliefs. Modelling each outcome with a family suited to its shape also separated the categorical from the graded components of the judgments, showing that the labels lowered both the probability of finding a work beautiful and its degree of beauty, shifted beliefs through the categorical choice alone, and left their residual effect at follow-up in the categorical component only.

## Limitations

All stimuli were genuine human paintings, which isolates the effect of belief but leaves open how labels interact with the features of actual AI-generated images; the AI label may also have been less plausible for some paintings than for others, although distrust of the manipulation was unrelated to the bias. The Forgery label described copies made to deceive, so its penalty may include a moral disapproval of fraud, and the AI label may likewise carry moral connotations, such as the appropriation of artists' work, which its association with attitudes toward AI does not separate from aesthetic expectations; a label describing an honest reproduction would isolate non-originality more cleanly. The labels did not cross syntheticness and authenticity: AI originals and AI copies were distinguished in the beliefs but not in the labels. The decomposition of the label effects on beliefs rests on assumptions that randomizing the label does not secure: appraisal was measured, not manipulated, and measurement error in the ratings would understate the indirect effects and overstate the direct ones. The pseudo-reveal of Phase 2 left the labels a partially valid cue, by design, so that the Phase 2 label effects cannot be read as a perseverance of beliefs. The follow-up confounded the passage of time with the correction, was completed by about two thirds of the sample, and was the only session in which self-relevance was measured.

## Conclusion

The devaluation of art attributed to AI combines a generic penalty for works that are not authentic originals, shared with human forgeries, with a larger penalty specific to the absence of a human author, which falls most heavily on the meaning a work is granted. This penalty is translated into beliefs about origin and reinforced by them, as viewers take beautiful and personally resonant works to be human-made, labelled or not. It is indifferent to the affective content and personal relevance of the work, and follows people's attitudes toward AI rather than their sensitivity to art or to their own body. Once the label is withdrawn and corrected, its effect on judgment fades, but the beliefs it induced outlast the memory of the label, and are later remembered as what the label said.
